input: This cost review takes a detailed look at the transport costs associated with a returns flow, which is an area of the operation that has attracted increasing attention in recent times. Each trip within the flow covers some 900 km, and the cost of the movement works out at $1.74 per km, taking into account the charges raised by the carrier for the work involved. Over the course of a year, the flow accounts for a total of 309 trips, and when all of these elements are brought together, the annual transport cost of the flow comes to $484k in total. It is worth noting that the figures used in this review are drawn from the carrier invoices for the last 12 months, so they reflect the amounts that were actually charged for the work over that period rather than any quoted or estimated rates. It should also be borne in mind that empty running is included in the trip count, which means that the trips recorded include the movements made by vehicles travelling without a load as part of the overall pattern of the flow, and the annual figure should be read with that coverage in mind when it is compared with other flows or carried forward into future planning.
target: The returns flow costs $484k per year (900 km per trip at $1.74 per km, 309 trips per year). The figure is assembled from the carrier invoices for the last 12 months, so it states what was charged for the work over that period, at the rates actually applied, rather than a quoted rate carried forward. Empty running is included in the trip count. The annual figure is therefore the cost of the whole movement cycle, loaded and empty running together, and it should be compared only with figures assembled on the same coverage: a flow costed on loaded trips alone would understate the same operation. Read on that basis, the figure gives operations management a settled baseline for the flow as it currently runs. Any change to the flow, in routing, in trip pattern or in carrier, can be costed against the baseline, provided the costing keeps the same coverage of empty running and the same invoice basis. A change that removes empty running would show against this baseline as a reduction in trips at the stated cost per kilometre; a change that only moves work between carriers would show as a change in the rate. The two kinds of saving are different in kind, and the baseline as stated keeps them separate. The baseline also fixes the questions that any proposal for change has to answer: which trips disappear, which kilometres shorten, or which rate changes, each stated against the same trip count and the same coverage.
